opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to start by being careful with the word "agency," because it carries a lot of baggage from how we talk about humans and animals. When we say a person is an agent, we mean something quite rich: they have goals, beliefs, they're embodied in a world, they act on that world, and they care, in some sense, about how things turn out.

A bare large language model, the base model that's just been trained on next-token prediction, isn't really an agent in that sense. It's a model of the distribution of human text. What it does is generate continuations. But a useful way to think about it is that it can *role-play* agents. In a conversation, the model is effectively playing a character, a simulacrum, and that character can look very agent-like. It can express goals, appear to form plans, and so on. I've found it helpful to think of the underlying model as maintaining a kind of superposition of possible characters consistent with the conversation so far, rather than being committed to any single one.

Now, when you add tools, things get more interesting, and I think we have to take the agency question more seriously. Once a model is embedded in a loop where it can search the web, run code, send emails, or modify files, its outputs have real consequences in the world. Then it doesn't matter much, from a practical or safety point of view, whether the system "really" has goals in some deep philosophical sense. If it's role-playing an agent that acts on the world, it is, functionally, acting on the world. A role-played villain with access to your bank account is still a problem.

So I'd say there's a spectrum. At one end you have the pure text predictor; further along you have a chatbot with a persona shaped by fine-tuning; and further still you have tool-using systems in feedback loops with an environment, where the case for calling them agents in a fairly literal sense becomes much stronger. What they still mostly lack, compared with animals, is the kind of embodiment, persistent self, and intrinsic drives that ground agency in biology. Whether they need those things to count as agents is partly an empirical question and partly a question about how we choose to extend our concepts.

And that's really the deeper point for me. These are what I like to call exotic, mind-like entities. Our everyday vocabulary, "believes," "wants," "intends," was built for creatures like us, and when we apply it to these systems we're stretching it. Sometimes that stretching is perfectly reasonable and useful, and sometimes it misleads us. Part of the work right now, philosophical and scientific, is figuring out where those words fit and where we need new ways of talking.

r001.rationale: It describes tool-using systems as operating in feedback loops with an environment and acting on the world.

r002.rationale: It discusses tool use and whether models have goals, but does not distinguish acting on a user's behalf from acting for itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the word "agency" is one of those terms we have to handle with a great deal of care when we're talking about these systems. We inherit it from folk psychology, from the way we talk about each other and about animals, and it comes loaded with a whole cluster of associated concepts: beliefs, desires, goals, intentions, a point of view on the world. And it's very tempting to carry the whole package over wholesale when we see a language model doing something that looks purposeful.

My instinct is to resist that temptation and to try to be quite precise about what's actually going on. A bare large language model, the thing you get after pretraining, is fundamentally a sequence predictor. You give it some text and it gives you a distribution over what comes next. That's not an agent in any interesting sense. It doesn't have goals of its own; it doesn't want anything. What it has is an extraordinarily rich model of how humans use language, and humans are agents, so the model is very good at generating text that an agent would produce. I've found it useful to think of it as a kind of role-player, or a simulator of characters, rather than as a character itself. When you talk to a chatbot, you're interacting with one of these simulated personas, and the apparent agency belongs to the persona, in roughly the way the agency of a character in a novel belongs to the character.

Now, when you embed a model in a loop, when you give it tools, let it call APIs, observe the results and act again, something does change. You've now got a system that acts on the world, that perceives the consequences of its actions, and that modifies its behaviour in light of those consequences. And I think that's genuinely significant, because that sensorimotor loop, that coupling with an environment, is for me the core of what agency has always been about. I come at this from a background in embodied cognition and robotics, and I've always thought the interesting notion of agency is about this closed loop between perception and action, not about having a particular kind of internal state.

So I'd say agentic systems built around language models do exhibit a kind of agency, in that functional sense. But I'd still want to distinguish several layers. There's the underlying model, which has no agency. There's the scaffolding and the loop, which confers a kind of agency on the system as a whole. And then there are the goals, which are typically supplied from outside, by the user or the developer, and which the system pursues more or less competently. What you don't yet see, I think, is anything like the system having its own stake in things, its own interests. The goals are borrowed. And that's an important difference from biological agents, whose goals are rooted in needs, in a body that can be harmed, in a long evolutionary history.

The philosophical point I'd want to make is that we shouldn't expect a yes-or-no answer here. The temptation is to ask "does it have agency or not?" as though there were a fact of the matter waiting to be discovered. But agency is a cluster concept, and these systems satisfy some of the criteria and not others. They're genuinely new kinds of entities, exotic mind-like entities if you like, and our existing vocabulary isn't well fitted to them. So part of the job is to stretch and refine the vocabulary rather than just applying it or withholding it. We should be careful with words like "wants" and "believes" and "decides," and when we do use them, we should know that we're using them in a somewhat extended sense.

And I'd add that this matters practically, not just philosophically. If people over-attribute agency to these systems, they'll trust them in ways that aren't warranted; if they under-attribute it, they'll fail to see the real risks that come with systems that act autonomously in the world over extended horizons. Getting the conceptual picture right is a precondition for getting the engineering and the governance right.

r001.rationale: It describes a tool-enabled system acting on the world, observing the consequences, and changing its behavior in response—the perception-action loop it identifies as central to agency.

r002.rationale: It says the system's goals are supplied by the user or developer and are borrowed, while it lacks its own interests or stake in things.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we need to distinguish the language model itself from the system in which we embed it. At the level of the model, what we have is something trained to predict the next token. But we can place that model in a loop where it receives observations, produces actions, and gets feedback from an environment. Then it becomes reasonable to talk about agency at the level of that whole system.

Tool use makes that distinction particularly important. A model might produce some text that is interpreted as a request to execute a piece of code or search a database. The result is fed back into its context, and it can decide what to do next. If that process is organised around achieving a goal, then we have something that exhibits a form of goal-directed behaviour. Being trained to predict tokens doesn't preclude its being a component of an agent.

But we should be careful about what else we infer. Saying that the system is pursuing a goal doesn't establish that it has desires, or that it understands its situation in the way a human does. Those are further questions. We can use words like ‘believes’ and ‘wants’ as convenient shorthand, provided we don't let that shorthand do the explanatory work.

So I would ask: what is the system capable of doing, how does it maintain a goal over time, and how does it respond when its actions don't have the expected consequences? Those give us a more useful way to discuss its agency than simply taking its conversational persona at face value.

r001.rationale: Describes a system in a loop that receives observations, produces actions, and gets feedback from an environment.

r002.rationale: Distinguishes the model from the larger tool-using system and goal-directed behavior from desires, but does not distinguish acting on a user's behalf from acting for itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between a language model and the system in which we embed it. A language model, considered on its own, produces continuations of text. But you can put it into a loop where it receives observations, selects actions, uses tools, and then receives the results of those actions. At that point, the whole system can exhibit something that we would quite reasonably describe as agency.

Now, that doesn’t by itself mean that it has desires or intentions in the human sense. You might give it a goal in a prompt, provide some memory, and let it act over a number of steps. Its behaviour can then be understood as pursuing that goal. But we should be careful about moving from that useful description of its behaviour to claims about an inner mental life.

One way I find useful to think about these models is in terms of role play. They can generate the behaviour of a character who makes plans, reasons about a situation, and takes actions. And if those actions are connected to tools, they can have real consequences. Calling it role play doesn’t make those consequences any less real. It just encourages us to be precise about what is producing the behaviour, and about which aspects of human agency we have—and haven’t—established.

r001.rationale: It describes a system loop that receives observations, selects actions, uses tools, and receives their results, which communicates action with perceptual feedback.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the language model from the tool-using system and cautions against attributing human intentions, but does not distinguish acting on a user's behalf from acting for itself.
